subtopic: FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE-EMBARGO RESTRICTIONS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE-EMBARGO RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Agriculture. Would the minister make a statement to the house as to whether any decisions were arrived at between Canadian agricultural officials and the United States department of agriculture authorities at a meeting held in Washington on Thursday and Friday of last week for the purpose of arriving at some clarification of the embargo restrictions placed on as a result of the foot-and-mouth disease?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE-EMBARGO RESTRICTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was good enough to furnish me with a copy of his question, to which I have prepared the following answer:
A group of Canadian officials went to Washington last week to meet United States officials to discuss problems related to foot-and-mouth disease. These discussions were arranged for two purposes: first, to exchange information regarding the quarantine and protective measures which are in force in both countries, and, second, to examine the effects upon trade of the import controls which have been imposed in both countries on livestock and related products. These meetings were informal and exploratory and were not for the purpose of negotiating commitments on the part of either government.
From the Canadian point of view the discussions were very informative and resulted in a clarification of the situation. All canned meats hermetically sealed and all cooked meats are not affected under the United States embargo. Some classes of boned-out meats, either cured or partially cooked, may also enter the United States under certain conditions.

subtopic: FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE-EMBARGO RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Agriculture whether under the restrictions imposed by Canada on the importation of meats from the United States, the same class and types of meats will be permitted entry into Canada as he has just told us are permitted entry into the United States, notwithstanding their embargo?

subtopic: FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE-EMBARGO RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: Yes, that would be true.

subtopic: ONTARIO AND SASKATCHEWAN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ONTARIO AND SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Resources and Development. Will the minister make a statement with respect to his last negotiations with the Ontario government for rental housing in the vicinity of Toronto?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development):
subtopic: ONTARIO AND SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough to give me notice of his question. I may say that during the last two months I have had discussions in Toronto with the Ontario government about problems of rental housing throughout the province under the terms of section 35 of the National Housing Act, that is, the section which provides for the federal-provincial partnership approach to the housing problem.
Inquiries of the Ministry
Both the Ontario government and the federal government realize that any comprehensive housing program for the province of Ontario should include rental housing for the greater Toronto area. My hon. friend will appreciate that the municipal problems of the greater Toronto area, involving availability of serviced land, schools, levels of tax rates, and so on, are complex. A number of suggestions were put forward during these conversations, and the Ontario government undertook to explore ways and means whereby section 35 might be implemented in greater Toronto. I expect to hear from them in this respect before long.

subtopic: ONTARIO AND SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I should like to ask a further question of the Minister of Resources and Development. Could he tell the house what progress he has made in negotiations with Saskatchewan to get housing started out there?

subtopic: ONTARIO AND SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a project for some 75 units in Moose Jaw has the concurrence of all levels of government, and the signing of the agreement is imminent.
I understand that in Regina a project for some 150 units-I am speaking from memory -is under negotiation.

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO HOURS OF SITTING

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
As we
have been setting up committees today it may be appropriate to ask the Prime Minister

House of Commons
if it is the government's intention to set up again the committee on rules which sat during the last session. Does the government propose to take some action on the recommendations contained in the report of the committee at the last session with respect to the hours of sitting?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
The government does not consider that it is the function of the government to take action with respect to rules of the house, which are under the control of members of the house.
Now, as to whether a committee should again be set up-that is a matter which has not been decided upon, but to which consideration can be given. I have had conversations with several of the members who composed that committee, and they seem to feel that what had been achieved was hardly compensation for the attention they had given to this work, and that unless there was some indication that there might be greater achievements than have been realized, it did not seem to be worth their while to devote more time to it.
However, I was not a member of the committee, and I have no opposition myself, personally, to its being set up again. If it is the desire of members of the house that it be reconstituted I will have no objection to making an opportunity for the matter to have consideration in the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question? Does the Prime Minister not feel that the implementation of what the committee recommended last year would in itself be compensation for the work we did?

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: I think if what was recommended by the committee could be accepted by the house, it would be an achievement. But it has been my understanding that there was no unanimity of view about that, except on one point, and that if it was brought before the house for discussion we would have little to show for it but the discussion.

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the committee was unanimous with respect to the proposed changes in the hours of sitting, will the government give consideration to allowing those changes to be made?

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
The government does not allow or disallow anything with respect to the hours of sitting of the house. That is a matter which is under the control of the house. Members of the government are also members of the house and they may have their views about it. I have spoken to several

about it-not just members of the government but other members of the house, and I have found objection to a shortening of the hours unless something else were done that would make it appear that shortening the hours would not lengthen the session.
I know that there are divergent views about this. Views have been expressed by others that we could have these shorter hours without doing anything about the length of speeches and still not prolong the session. But there seems to be no general agreement in that regard. I know that the hon. member has his views as to what would be desirable, and I have mine, but we are only two of 262 members, and we cannot always have our way.
I was told that the thing that would have to be done to follow the traditions of the house was, first, to have a motion that the report prepared during the last session be considered during this session. If that were agreed to, then a motion could be introduced referring the whole matter to the committee of the whole house. It did not appear to me that if we referred it to the committee of the whole house we would get very far beyond a lot of, no doubt, most interesting speeches.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this is a
matter of some importance, and of obvious interest to the whole house, I suggest that the Prime Minister should not leave the impression that his position in a matter of this kind is simply that of a single member of the house. Both under the rules of the house and by virtue of the very evident willingness of members of the party to which he belongs to support his statements in this house, there is no suggestion that his position is the same as that of a private member. So far as that is concerned, a private member cannot bring forward this motion. This motion can be brought forward by the government at any time, and it does not need to be a motion to approve the report that was introduced in the last session.
I think all that hon. members who have raised this question are asking is that there be a motion to refer the matter to a committee. With the knowledge of what has occurred, that committee could probably bring in a report in a very short time. In spite of the delays that government supporters are creating at this time in other fields of discussion, I believe that in this case the committee could bring in a report very quickly and place before the house views which could be approved or disapproved.

May I suggest to the Prime Minister that we deal with this matter in terms of reality, and recognize that if this matter is to be considered at all it must be initiated by the government? While it is not the responsibility of the government to say what shall be done, a committee should be given a chance to recommend to this house what the representatives of all the parties agree can be done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
I will ask the gentleman who acts as our whip to confer with those who represent the other groups in the house, and if they can agree on such a committee I shall be glad to provide an opportunity for the house to pass upon their suggestion. I shall do that just as soon as I can get a report from them as to what seems to be the desire of hon. members in that regard.
Dealing with the other point, I should be only too happy to suggest what might in my view-I have not had as great experience as some other hon. members, not having been here so long-be helpful for the conduct of the business of the house. But in view of the fact, as the hon. gentleman has said, that there is a large majority of members in the house who usually agree with me, I have always hesitated to expose hon. members and myself to the charge that we were steamrolling things through the house. That we do not wish to do. If through the good offices of the gentlemen who represent the different groups in the house we can get at something % that will not appear to be an imposition upon any minority group, I shall be most happy to provide the occasion for the house to deal with it.

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome that
suggestion. May I point out that far from saying that the Prime Minister was doing anything that could be interpreted as operating a steamroller, I was merely suggesting that he provide a vehicle by which the members themselves could give expression to their different ideas as to what they wanted to do.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, March 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. E. W. George for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Fair.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from what I have heard in this house at times it seems to me that some hon. members are not aware that Nova Scotians are very
The Address-Mr. Balcom hardy people. If we were not so hardy I am afraid we would have been pushed into the Atlantic years ago. The weaker members of our community migrate to Ontario, where the competition is not so keen, and in a short time they become heads of universities or of great financial institutions. Some even find their way to British Columbia and return to Ottawa as members of parliament.
In the course of a day a great many problems are presented to a member of parliament. Many of them are individual or group problems which have no real bearing on public policy. A great many are the result of the increasing government activity in the life of the nation. This has been increasingly marked with the need to devote a greater proportion of our resources to defence. But apart from such expenditures, which we hope are to some extent temporary, but which although temporary have nevertheless curtailed the extension of other services such as public works and social services, the government has gone a long way in the field of social security. This aspect of public policy is here to stay, but its relative newness, together with the huge defence expenditures, has helped to create problems which go to the heart of our system of government.
The most disturbing aspect of this matter is the growing tendency for individuals and groups to look to the government to bail them out of difficulties that arise or to provide them with special benefits for some reason, all of which become precedents for others in like situations to follow. I would suggest that there are probably a few members in the house who have a tendency to take advantage of precedents that have been so established. This government has an outstanding record in the field of social security. Our present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is truly conscious of the needs of our people, and his co-operation is reflected across Canada in the many good works sponsored by his department. The most important recent step, of course, was the implementation of universal old age pensions. Hardly less important, although less widespread, is the increase in the veterans pension; and now we hope for a sympathetic and understanding consideration of war veterans allowances for burnt-out soldiers.
These are steps which I think have had the support of most Canadians. There is criticism, of course-some on the basis that the timing only increased inflationary pressure, others on the basis that the old age pension of $40 was not large enough. That, however, is a healthy sign, for opposition, freely expressed, is part and parcel of our way of life. These measures are consonant with our
53S

The Address-Mr. Balcom industrial development and are quite in keeping with the abundance of our resources.
One of the most difficult problems of a member of parliament is to keep first things first in dealing with the many problems that are brought to his attention. The way of least resistance, of course, is to espouse the causes which are backed by strong organizations. The danger in this course is obvious, for its corollary is political weakness where organization is lacking, resulting too often in neglect when public policy is wanting.
Progress has been made in the past few years both in organization and in the recognition by government of the problems of the fishing industry. But there is a considerable group which has no association to speak for it and whose problems are quickly supplanted in the public eye by causes more vigorously pressed.
I am speaking particularly of the inshore fishermen who live in the communities which dot the shores of Halifax county-indeed of the whole coast line of Nova Scotia-and who lack organization. Granted that their way of life is one of independence and that the nature of their craft, with its reliance on skill and courage, is eminently suited to the exercise of individual initiative. Yet surely the farmers, if we may judge from those in the house, have not lost their independence by building up strong federations.
A perennial cause of dissatisfaction among these fishermen is the spread between the price they receive for fish and the price the consumer pays. This controversial question of "price spread" is complicated, and I have not the information to make a conclusive judgment. It has been contended after past investigations that rather than unreasonable profits to "middlemen", as is commonly held, the major cause of the low return to the fishermen is inefficiency in handling and distributing by our transportation system. The nature of the product in this case makes it peculiarly liable to spoilage and presents special technical problems in transportation and distribution. Yet other industries have solved similar problems. These would not be insurmountable if tackled with sufficient vigour, financial backing and organization, I am sure. Here is where the leadership of a strong trade association would be effective and could compensate to some extent for the difficulties of small producers in competition with mass production industries.
It may be said that it is no concern of the government whether or not the industry has lacked ardent spokesmen and been politically weak. I contend that by so much the more should the government recognize


its problems. The industry has over the years been traditionally between the hammer and the anvil: the old familiar problem of maritime industry of high cost supplies, gear and equipment bought in a protected market on the one hand, and highly competitive selling in the world market on the other.
There has been some adjustment in the industry as a whole in the past few years. A larger proportion of production is now going to the North American market, and there has been a period of relative stability. And on the basis of resources and market possibilities, further expansion on a profitable basis is possible-given, of course, improved equipment and facilities.
This is an industry which can be developed further to the very great advantage of the maritime provinces. A relatively minor expenditure on further research, both scientific and economic, and active development, would pay handsome dividends. It would be not a question of subsidy or special assistance on the basis of expediency, but a wise investment. We have found that so often national policies for development of other parts of Canada have redounded to the disadvantage of the maritimes. Surely it is not too much to ask for adequate attention to the development of these rich resources, lying right at our door, which other people come across an ocean to exploit-and at a profit, too!
I feel that much remains to be done, but I do want to commend the government for the increasing attention given to the fisheries industry in the past few years. In co-operation with the provinces, training has been provided. Shore facilities, such as bait freezing plants on a small scale, have been established; loan capital has been made available through provincial loan boards for procuring boats and equipment. But unfortunately these loans are not such that they can be given to the small inshore fisherman who can provide himself with only a small boat and cannot afford a larger one. Capable research people are working both on fish resources, and processing and handling, and the plant in Halifax is not only the best in Canada, I am given to understand, but one of the finest, in work results, in the world-that is in work results; I do not mean in equipment particularly.
Yet I feel that we have not yet reached the fundamental problem of the individual fisherman, that is, to increase his productivity-by increasing his capital equipment- in such a way that he is in a position to cope with the risks of the trade. Nor have we solved the financial and technical problems of satisfactory marketing facilities

which are fundamental to the industry as a whole. A more radical approach to both phases of the problem may be called for. For lack of initiative or imagination on our part let us not sell these fishing communities short and permit an important resource to go by default to those countries with superior know-how.
The problems of the fishing industry in Nova Scotia were ably set out and presented on Tuesday by the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth (Mr. Kirk), and by my colleague, the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey), and by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) on Wednesday. But I should like to add to the list of losses of those in the western counties the losses in the immediate vicinity of Halifax. Our information is that 6,126 lobster traps were lost in the recent storms, and at the value placed upon them by the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth that loss would be some $40,000. Some communities were hit harder than others. For instance at Devil's island, a small island off the mouth of Halifax harbour which is exposed to the winter rigours of the Atlantic, thirty-six fishermen lost an estimated 2,300 traps of the 2,500 that were in the water. That was a paralysing blow. At the small village of Sambro, to the west, twenty fishermen lost approximately 1,000 traps. As I said before, this leaves the fishermen with practically no resources, and with neither cash nor credit at the bank.
In addition to the hazards of wind, ice and storms, these fishermen face other dangers. I shall refer to only one; that is the risk taken by our fishermen during the war when submarines operated off our harbours and in the bay of Fundy. In the latter instance spies were landed on our shores; and the presence of submarines in our waters was first learned by our fishermen, who I have no doubt were used by naval headquarters in order to obtain information. In spite of the menace, however, the fishermen continued their work and daily faced a watery grave. Nothing could scare them off the sea. Of all our citizens none are more loyal than the fishermen. When wars break out, almost the first to enlist are these same fishermen, who join the navy and merchant marine as captains, skippers, crewmen and pilots.
I am looking forward to the time when government experts will devise, as they have in other occupations, a cheap form of insurance for fishermen on their gear and equipment, and a means by which the fishermen may enjoy the benefits of unemployment insurance and compensation. I am afraid a great many members of this house are not aware that at present fishermen are not
The Address-Mr. Balcom entitled to unemployment insurance and these other benefits. With other hon. members I respectfully suggest to the government that an exhaustive inquiry be made into these matters on behalf of the fishermen, and soon. We are not asking for a subsidy for our products but merely for an investment in maritime economy; for I contend, Mr. Speaker, that our Canadian pattern of life is made strong by all the complex forces involved and co-operating in it. The active part in our national life played by the fishing folk of this country cannot be overestimated, and they should be taken out of the class of forgotten people.
Haligonians generally are very appreciative of the co-operation they have received from the ministers. Particularly are they grateful to the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), who has done many things for us. I refer particularly to the fact that the historic sites branch of his department has taken control of the historic Halifax citadel, known as Fort George. Already we can see great changes in this structure, in that the old moat with its stone and iron work is being preserved.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and to extend to him the thanks of the people of Halifax for the assurance of his co-operation with the city in the establishment of an airport. The position of Halifax in the national communications system is important, and I might also say unique. As it is the main land terminus of air, rail and water transportation, there must be adequate and flexible facilities for commercial as well as defence needs. But this same terminal position involves rather heavy costs in relation to revenue, and it has not been easy to obtain and maintain adequate services. The minister has recognized that it is in the national interest to maintain and improve transportation facilities. The proposed arrangements regarding the Halifax airport are in line with this policy. Such a port as ours is vitally necessary not only for commerce but as an alternative in time of emergency to the naval airport at Eastern Passage.
While I am on the subject of transportation facilities I should like to draw attention to the inadequacy of hotel accommodation in the city of Halifax. In 1930 the Canadian National Railways built the Nova Scotian hotel, a structure of 170 rooms. At the same time the citizens of Halifax in a community effort built the Lord Nelson hotel with 200 rooms. Today the Nova Scotian hotel is completely inadequate to meet the demands of the travelling public or of the patrons of the Canadian

The Address-Mr. Balcom National Railways, Canadian National Steamships, or Trans-Canada Air Lines. With ship travel increasing every year from this port I would urge the minister to give the question of adding another 100 rooms to this hotel his earnest consideration.
Alongside this too small but none the less fine and well-operated hotel are the outmoded express sheds adjoining the Canadian National station. These sheds are of wood and were built, if I remember correctly, about the time of the first war. They are not only a potential fire hazard; they are unsightly, and should be replaced.
On March 31 Halifax is to have the pleasure of a visit by the Minister of Transport, who will officially open the new pier 3 which replaces one burned out many years ago. The completion of this pier will greatly assist in the efficient handling of freight, but the port facilities are by no means rounded out by this structure. The old pier 4 is at present in very bad repair, and will need to be reconstructed in the very near future so that freight to Newfoundland and Europe may be expedited.
Almost every day in this house we hear of grade A hogs, grade A cattle, No. 1 wheat and everything else coming out of the west. So I was somewhat surprised to learn through the columns of the Halifax Herald of March 6 that Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia had a greater percentage of grade A hogs in their shipments to market than any other Canadian provinces, according to the latest tests by the federal Department of Agriculture. Like so many things produced in the maritime provinces, we have not the quantity but we surely have the quality.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, is it too much to ask that we should have a greater unity in objectives in this Canada of ours? Is it too much to ask -that our ten provinces aim their policies at what is good for the whole, and that the federal government in turn act in the same way toward the units that make up this wonderful country? It was only last week that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), speaking in this house, stressed the f-act that we have a great country and a great people, and of course we all agree with that. A former Canadian statesman once said that Canada was like a string of beads, but he qualified that by saying they were not all pearls. If such is the case I would-suggest that those provinces which might not be classed as pearls be brought to equality with the others, so that we may -all be considered of the same value. So far as humanly possible any bars between provinces should be discarded. We should start at once at the top, and by that I mean by having

reciprocity in education. Where education is of equal standard, professional degrees granted in one province should qualify a graduate to practise his profession in another. I am sure that this would end the overcrowding of a profession in one province; in fact I feel we would never have to meet that condition. We should, Mr. Speaker, see that all citizens in this country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, are entitled to receive the same opportunities and privileges.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that all members in this house have listened attentively to the member for Halifax (Mr. Balcom) who has just taken his seat. There was very little in what he said with which anyone could disagree. I am heartily in accord with practically everything he said. I agree with his remarks about our social services. He mentioned the fact that his party had brought in most of the social services in this country. I would point out to him that old age pensions, -children's allowances and all social service matters that have been introduced in this country have had the full support not only of every party in this house but of every member.
I agree also with the hon. member's desire that the fishermen of his province, as well as those of the other maritime provinces, receive more consideration. My constituency is not directly interested in fishing, and is one of the few in the maritime provinces that is not. There -are three -constituencies out of ten in New Brunswick that do not touch the sea. All the other constituencies in New Brunswick, in Nova Scotia and in Prince Edward Island, as well -as those in- the province of Newfoundland, are interested in fishing; they -all border on the sea. Mention of that fact indicates how necessary it is that -this great industry in the maritime provinces receive -the -consideration which is its due.
Another matter has been- mentioned during the last few days, particularly by members from the province of Saskatchewan, upon which I desire to make a few comments. Saskatchewan is greatly concerned over the fact that it will lose some four or five members in the redistribution. We all sympathize with this great province, because I look for important developments there in the future. I do not think that they need to worry too much, because if they lose members today I am satisfied that a few years from now they will regain their members, especially if the developments which have been sponsored by certain members, such as the South Saskatchewan river development, occur. This will mean much to the economy of that province in the future. I would not

be surprised if Saskatchewan were to compete with Alberta in days to come also in the development of oil.
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure) mentioned yesterday that one member thought it unfair that Prince Edward Island should have four members when other provinces with much larger populations in proportion were losing members. I should like to point out to those members that our maritime provinces, particularly New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, were two of the pillars of confederation. In 1874 New Brunswick had 16 members; today it has 10 members. In the same year Nova Scotia had 21 members; today it has 13 members and I believe is to be reduced to 12. While the Saskatchewan members are feeling sorry for themselves, I would point out to them that throughout the years the maritime provinces have seen their populations decreased and have lost representatives in this house, just as Saskatchewan expects to lose representatives now. In 1874 the maritime provinces had 43 members, but today we have 27.
As a New Brunswicker, and because I feel he deserves it, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. George), the mover of the address, and also the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John). I expect these hon. members are now beginning to feel bored: with these congratulatory remarks. However, they are deserved. The member for Westmorland said that it was not altogether a compliment to him when he was chosen for this task, but it was a compliment to his constituency. No doubt that is a fact. I feel it was also a compliment to my province of New Brunswick. In looking over the record I find that this is the first time in many, many years that a member from that province has been asked either to move or to second the address. We are glad to see that we are receiving some recognition, even if it is only in this small matter.
One item in the speech from the throne which interested me very much, and which has already been the subject of comment by a number of members, is the mention of legislation to be brought down in connection with the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Veterans Benefit Act. I am pleased that these matters are to receive attention. I want to say here that personally I feel they should have received attention some time ago. I could not understand why, when the old age pensions and veterans pensions were dealt with at the last session, these matters were not dealt with at the same time. The veterans from one end of this country to the other could not understand the delay either, because nothing has been gained by it. I
The Address-Mr. Brooks feel that a great injustice has been done to many of our veterans, especially those on small pensions. The small pensioner, who also received war veterans allowance, did not get any benefits from the increased pension if he was receiving $610 as a single man or $1,100 as a married man. He could not understand it. I am pleased to see that a veterans committee is to be set up, and I hope that this injustice in the War Veterans Allowance Act will be corrected.
My main object in speaking this afternoon is to support the appeal which was made by the member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) with reference to the expansion of the port of Saint John. Perhaps I have not the same interest in the city of Saint John that the hon. member has, but I might say that my constituency touches the Saint John river and is only a few miles from the city of Saint John. There is no constituency in the province of New Brunswick which benefits more from trading with that city than does the constituency of Royal. We supply them with their dairy products. Practically all the milk that is consumed in the city of Saint John comes from my constituency, and when the city of Saint John is prosperous the people of my constituency and the people of other parts of the province of New Brunswick are prosperous.
It would mean much to us if in our province we had a city twice the size of Saint John. That is one reason why we are jealous of anything which seems to detract or take away from it. I may say that we are very proud of the city of Saint John, the first incorporated city in the Dominion of Canada. It is one of our oldest cities. It has been a great seaport from the very early days of the history of this country. Ships and the sea have been a part of Saint John since the days of Champlain, Latour and other earlier discoverers of this country. Saint John is also one of the few cities that have been mentioned in prose and poetry. I am not going to quote any poetry this afternoon, but two of the great poets of this country were born in my province. I refer to Bliss Carman, probably the greatest poet of Canada, and his cousin, Sir Charles G. D. Roberts. Both wrote poetry on ships and the port of Saint John. Before confederation it was a great port and a great shipbuilding centre. After confederation we were told that our city was to be the Liverpool of Canada. Sir John A. Macdonald said at that time that the commerce going from ports of the maritimes would bring prosperity to these provinces such as they never had before. When speaking in the city of Saint John in 1897, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said that he would never be satisfied until every pound of Canadian

The Address-Mr. Brooks freight was carried through Canadian ports. That has been the ideal and the objective of the ports of Saint John and Halifax. I am sorry to say that the dream of Sir John has never been fulfilled, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier's promise or hope that every pound of freight would go through the ports of Saint John and Halifax has not been realized. We had to fight and fight all the way to get the freight which originates in the west, and in different parts of Canada, from being shunted off to ports like Portland and Boston and other ports of the United States. It has been a continual fight for these two cities of Saint John and Halifax.
We have been quite successful. Today Saint John and Halifax are enjoying a very busy winter. They are enjoying considerable export from these cities, but there is fear today that on account of lack of suitable accommodation and port facilities they are going to lose a certain amount of this business and that it will again be diverted to ports in the United States. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read a short paragraph from an article in the Times-Globe of Saint John, published on March 12 of this year. In speaking about the situation in the port of Saint John that paper said:
At the present time, the inability of the port of Saint John to handle the normal flow of business is causing loss of potential wages to many harbour front workers. Vessels are being diverted in some cases to other ports to avoid long waits for docking accommodation, because each day's delay is very expensive to the shipping lines.
That is something that should not be permitted to happen. On account of the lack of port facilities the diversion of ships may again take place and ships will be sent to Portland or to some other United States city. I do not wish to weary the house, but I have here a letter which comes from the Saint John board of trade. It is not too long, and it sets out very clearly the situation in the port of the city of Saint John at the present time. I may say that this is one of forty letters which were sent out by the board of trade of Saint John to the different members who visited that city last winter, and who, I am sure, have very pleasant memories of their visit. This letter is from the president of the Saint John board of trade and reads as follows:
Mr. A. J. Brooks, M.P.,
Royal, New Brunswick,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Brooks:
We did so enjoy your visit with us during March of last year, and as I drove down Germain street this morning I did so wish that you could be back

with us to see the emergency situation existing in our port. Each and every dock working to capacity, and seven ocean-going freighters anchored outside the harbour warned that there would be a five-day delay before they could dock. Each containing cargo important to our Canadian economy in one province or another.
This situation is urgent and terribly important to the city of Saint John, the province of New Brunswick and all Canada. There is no criticism of port management nor national harbours board. A wonderful job is being done under the conditions.
To fulfil our part we must have something now more than replacements and the proper authorities have full details where expansion could be made with speed this summer.
We are attaching a mimeographed copy of a recent editorial in our local paper where it is correctly pointed out that, not only the Canadian effort, but the entire economy of our province of New Brunswick is adversely affected by lack of proper facilities in our port, which facilities we had great pleasure in showing you one year ago.
Our member, Mr. D. A. Riley, has brought this matter to the floor of the house, and the Hon. Mr. Chevrier has expressed knowledge and appreciation of the situation but, according to press report this morning, advised Mr. Riley that he does not make government policy.
We know that one minister in the government does not make government policy; we also know that a minister in charge of a department recommends policy regarding his own department, and that is what we hope the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) will do. I continue with the letter:
We have had marvellous replacements but not a single additional dock in twenty years.
That is a long time ago. Twenty years ago there was a fire in the city of Saint John and the docks were destroyed. As is pointed out here, a considerable sum was spent in that port, but it was only for the replacement of the docks that were there twenty years ago. The letter continues:
There is another replacement contemplated, which is fine as far as it goes, but what this port needs is increased facilities by extension of present piers that will permit us to do our part. In other words, all we ask is "Give us the tools."
On behalf of our board, to you who actually visited the port of Saint John and travelled in our harbour, may I ask and urge your support of Mr. Riley in helping the Hon. Mr. Chevrier by voicing your support on the floor of the house, resulting in order in council, or whatever parliamentary procedure may be necessary, so that increased berthage needed in the port of Saint John be recognized as part of Canada's defence effort and national economy and implemented without delay.
I am trying to make this letter as brief as possible, but I could give you figures on very short notice of the very poor publicity our port is receiving because of delays to all shipping companies whose ships are on very tight schedules. I could give you figures of ships on such tight schedules that this port is losing because they cannot wait, and I can show you letters to shipping agents here, from shippers who are cancelling further shipments from this port. Possibly lost altogether to Canada.
Our board of trade will sincerely appreciate your active interest in this effort, in which we have the

complete support of the premier and legislature of the province of New Brunswick, the mayor and councillors of the city of Saint John.
Our all-year-round port is important not only to us, but to all Canada.
Kindest personal regards.
G. G. Anglin
President.
That letter speaks in most eloquent terms of the situation, and it is not necessary for me to comment on it any further, but I should like to point out that this fear of diversion of trade is not something new. We have heard it discussed in this House of Commons many times. I have heard Mr. D. King Hazen, the former member from the city of Saint John, bring this matter to the attention of the house. Hon. members will recall that in 1948 there was a possibility of our losing certain ships from Halifax and Saint John- in fact, we did lose some. Mr. Hazen brought the matter up as a result of a statement made by Mr. R. C. Vaughan, who was then president of the Canadian National Railways. Mr. Hazen at that time quoted a statement by Mr. Vaughan, and said:
To give the story from the beginning I want to refer to an Associated Press dispatch from Portland, Maine, dated July 23 last, which quoted Mr. R. C. Vaughan, president of the Canadian National Railways, as saying in an interview that the C.N.R. has "a big stake" in Portland, and that "we're going to do everything we can for the port of Portland."
That was what precipitated Mr. Hazen's remarks at that time. I might add that there had been a number of telegrams from the municipalities of Saint John and Halifax. The mayors of those cities as well as the boards of trade had written or wired in to the Minister of Transport.
I wish to bring out particularly that in reply to a wire from the mayor of Saint John complaining about the loss of ships to Halifax and Saint John, the minister sent the following wire, as it is set out at page 944 of Hansard for 1948:
I have your telegram referring to statement alleged to have been made by R. C. Vaughan, president of Canadian National Railways, which I have not seen. Please let me assure you that statements of policy always emanate from the government or one of its ministers.
He was not so definite at that time that it came from the government, but said it emanated either from the government or from one of its ministers. The telegram continues:
The policy of the government is to encourage and assist its national ports to the fullest extent, further, to use the facilities of our national ports to the maximum and to increase those facilities when required.
I call attention to that statement, that it is to increase those facilities when required.
The Address-Mr. Brooks That is exactly what we are asking at the present time. There can be no question that further facilities are needed. All we are asking is that, since they are required, the minister and the government see that they are furnished. The telegram continues:
In evidence of this the government has spent from 1936 to 1946, for capital and reconstruction of our national ports, approximately $18 million. This year's estimate for the port of Saint John contains initial appropriations which will mean eventual expenditure within a year or two of approximately $3 million.
As I said before, f am certain that $3 million was spent for the rebuilding of facilities that had been burned. Then, continuing the quotation:
National harbours board informs me surveys are under way for further expansion. All of which is an indication that government has very much in mind the development and expansion of facilities at the port of Saint John.
I am sorry the minister is not in his seat, because I should have liked to ask him, in connection with the last part of this telegram, what is being done at the present time. It will be noted that he says that the national harbours board had informed him that surveys were under way for further expansion, and that this was an indication that the government had very much in mind the development and expansion of facilities at the port of Saint John.
There can be no question that, through the national harbours board, the government is well aware of the situation in the harbour of Saint John. Upon reading the telegram of the minister in 1948, there is no doubt in my mind that surveys have been made and that, so far as this government is concerned, all that is required at the present time is to vote money to develop these much needed facilities in Saint John, and to carry out the plans which I am sure the harbours board must have at the present time.
I do not think it is necessary for me to argue the point at greater length. The situation is obvious. It was obvious to the forty members who went to Saint John last year from this House of Commons. It was the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) himself who pointed out certain piers that were in a bad state of repair, to the point of being useless.
We have the record from the board of trade and from the press that ships cannot find berths in Saint John, and that as a result they are being diverted to other ports. We learn that the longshoremen are losing their wages and their employment, and that in all probability this business is going to the United States.
542	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Bruneau
Halifax and Saint John are always recognized in times of war. In two world wars they have played a great part in the defence of this country. No cities in Canada have done more for the defence of the country and of liberty than have Saint John and Halifax. In times of peace they should not be forgotten. I can recall that during the last two wars there were always bottlenecks at Halifax and Saint John, so far as shipping was concerned. We are spending billions of dollars on defence. I say a proper defence of the country requires that we should have ports from which we can readily ship our supplies overseas in a time of need.
The repairing and building of ports is not like the making of tanks or aeroplanes. If a war comes, then we have these ports we can use; and when the war is over those facilities remain and can be used for the development of the country in times of peace.
I am sorry, as I said, that the minister is not in his seat this afternoon. I do hope however that he will listen to the pleas of the people in the old port of Saint John, and see that justice is done so far as that port is concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I was deeply interested in the historical facts given by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. George) with respect to his riding.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted also to extend my sincere congratulations to my friend, the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Gauthier), on his splendid description of the natural resources of his county.
(Text):
At the beginning of this sixth session of the twenty-first parliament, history is in the making. We are now mourning the loss of our beloved sovereign, George VI, who with his charming wife toured our great country in 1939, leaving everywhere a deep-rooted impression that he was indeed our king, the king of Canada. We shall long remember him, not as an important personage, but as a great king and a good citizen. His passing will be regretted not only here in Canada and in the British empire, but in all free countries of the world.
To the members of his family, to the queen mother, to Queen Mary, to Queen Elizabeth II and to Princess Margaret Rose I
[Mr. Brooks.)

wish, in the name of those whom I have the privilege of representing in the house, to extend my heartfelt sympathy.
To our gracious sovereign, Queen Elizabeth II, we wish to give the assurance of our loyalty, while expressing the hope that hers will be a fruitful reign. It seems only yesterday that we had the opportunity of greeting her in our country as the heir to the throne. As in the case of her parents, her visit strengthened the bonds that bind our people to the British queen.
Among the outstanding events that have taken place recently is the departure of the former governor general, Lord Alexander of Tunis. When he left our shores we had the impression that we were losing one of our own. We are thankful to those who made him a member of the privy council. About two years ago when Lord Alexander paid a visit to our riding he was cheered by the people of Plantagenet, Alfred, L'Orignal and Hawkesbury. When in his farewell speech he spoke of his deep and sincere love for our country my constituents, among others, really understood his sympathy for and the attachment to those whom he had so faithfully served during his term of office in Canada.
Another important event which will long be remembered in Canadian history was the appointment of one of our native sons as the representative of Her Majesty in Canada, the Right Hon. Vincent Massey. As the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) explained so ably in the house, this appointment of a Canadian to represent the British crown will in no way weaken our attachment and loyalty to Queen Elizabeth, the queen. It was thought that to entrust these functions to one of our own was to express a deeper and closer bond to the sovereign of Canada. I am sure no happier choice could have been made. The fact that His Excellency the Governor General presided over the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences undoubtedly places him in a better position to understand our position.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Cote) upon his appointment as Postmaster General. I wish also to congratulate my colleague, the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey), upon his recent appointment as parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe).
During his recent visit to Ottawa the Right Hon. Winston Churchill stated that our Prime Minister had played a major part in enacting the North Atlantic treaty. The meetings recently held at Lisbon have made clear to the whole world the determination of free countries to work together in perfect

harmony for the safeguarding of our democratic liberties and for the welfare and prosperity of the peoples of the North Atlantic pact.
The courage of our boys of the 25th brigade, our men of the navy and of the 426th squadron of the R.C.A.F., at present in service in the Pacific, undoubtedly testifies to the determination of our people to hold a place among those great nations who willingly lend a helping hand to oppressed countries. Among those, let us not forget the soldiers of the 27th brigade which has now taken its place among the armies of the NATO countries in Europe.
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to represent here what I think is one of the most interesting ridings in the eastern part of the province of Ontario, the county of Prescott, halfway between the metropolis and the capital, in the midst of what is known as the golden triangle of the Ottawa valley with its rich farmlands.
Prescott is the largest cheese producing county of the British empire. In view of its geographical position, between the St. Lawrence and the Ottawa rivers, we are expecting a great industrial impetus from the development of the St. Lawrence seaway. I should like to add, as has previously -been stated, that my riding offers great possibilities to those who are anxious to set up industries in our region, thus helping to implement the program of industrial decentralization.
Our farmers, like those of other rural ridings, rely on government assistance to maintain production at a peak. With the price of pork now at a very low level, the agricultural associations are most anxious that the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) set a minimum price at about $30 per hundredweight. Far from being opposed to subsidies granted to the western farmers, I feel that they need: every bit of assistance we can give them, but I should like to make sure that the dairy farmers in the eastern part of our country are given their good share so as to enable them to maintain the stability of Canadian economy.
I should like to remind the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) that there are two airports in our riding, one at St. Eugene and the other at Pendleton, which could, I am sure, serve a better purpose. Quite a number of young men were trained there during the last war under the commonwealth air training plan. I would appreciate very much if the minister would have a few experts in his department look into the possibility of reopening those airports.
The Address-Mr. Bruneau
I would also like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) a matter which is of primary importance to the people of my riding. The Nation river will soon, as in previous years, create havoc over a considerable area in the southwestern tip of Prescott county. I am given to understand that if a channel of about an acre's length, 7 feet deep by 180 feet wide, were dug near the C.P.R. bridge, close to the railway station at Plantagenet, this flood could be kept in check, because the Scotch river and other tributaries emptying into the Nation at that point would follow this channel, which would be deep enough to hold the excess water. Large blocks of ice carried by this water and left on the fields also cause considerable damage. I am told that several years ago one of the farmers of that region suffered a loss of about $3,500 because of such a flood.
I hope that the Minister of Public Works will take good note of the precarious situation in which the farmers of the Plantagenet area find themselves and will see fit to allot the funds required to undertake this work which would certainly not be so very costly.
My people are grateful to the government for the social security measures passed by this house. Last year, two such bills were enacted: the Old Age Security Act for all people of seventy and the federal-provincial old age pension scheme for those between 65 and 69, with the means test. I think we legislators would be well advised to add to such social security measures another form of assistance, that is, pensions to invalids.
Since the beginning of this parliament every time it has been possible I have advocated such a pension here in this house. Every time we have to cope with the problem of a handicapped person who is unable to provide his own means of subsistence, we have to explain to him that there exists a form of assistance for a good many people but that in his case there is no means of providing for him. I sincerely hope that it will be possible during this present session to attend to the needs of those unfortunate people. Just as we are helping our older citizens, likewise should we also help the invalids.
It is also our duty to lend a helping hand to our young people, the citizens of tomorrow. I would like to see studied the possibility of setting up a committee, the main purpose of which would be assistance to our young people on a federal scale. I should think that while implementing the recommendations of the royal commission on arts, letters and sciences, something could be done in the way of helping our young folk who are certainly not without possibilities,

Events are shaping every day and little do we know of what can happen while we are here legislating. Let us ask the help of Divine Providence so that we may each, in his own way, make a better country to live in and help to the utmost the people living in countries where the government is no longer for the people by the people. Let us spare nothing so that those who are persecuted, those who are living behind the iron curtain, may one day see a ray of light. Nor let us forget those at home, the disabled ones who are entitled to a place in society. In this way we, the representatives of the people, will have fulfilled the task we had set ourselves and feel the satisfaction of a duty well done.

We are still disappointed that, so far as the speech from the throne would seem to indicate, nothing is to be done at this session. The need is there and the time for action on health insurance is now.
The particular reason why I felt I must get back into this debate relates to the fact that no clear statement has yet been made with regard to the making of recoveries from the estates of old age pensioners who were in receipt of the old age pension up to December 31, 1951, under the former Old Age Pensions Act. Let me indicate that in respect of certain groups of people the picture is clear. It is perfectly clear that there are to be no recoveries with respect to pensions paid under the Old Age Security Act. They are completely free of any means test, any debt, any recovery, or any lien of any kind. That applies not only in the case of those who have come on the new old age security pension since January 1, 1952, but it is also clear that, in the case of a person who was on the former pension prior to December 31, 1951, and has been transferred to the new pension, there can be no recovery against his estate with respect to the amounts of

money he is receiving now or any amounts of money he has received since January 1, 1952.
There is another group with respect to whom the picture is clear, namely those who receive pensions under the Old Age Assistance Act, or in other words the pension paid to those between 65 and 69, on a fifty-fifty basis, with a means test and all that. Despite its other shortcomings, that pension does not involve the attachment of any property in any way. There is no debt due either to the provincial or federal governments so far as that pension is concerned. No liens are placed against any property and no recoveries can be made out of the estates of any persons who have received that pension, which likewise began as at January 1, 1952.

I will agree that in part what the minister has said indicates the situation, but it does not tell the whole story. The minister suggests that the federal government has no responsibility at all for this. In the first place the whole problem of recoveries against estates arose out of a provision in the federal act. It was in the first act that was drawn up back in the middle twenties, and it was in the new version that
fMr. Knowles.]
we got in 1947. The provincial authorities are acting on the basis of what they believe to be the interpretation of that act and of the agreements they signed. Some of the provinces take one view of that agreement while some take an opposite view.
This is not the first time this issue has come up. It came up back in 1943 and 1944 in particular. I know whereof I speak; I was here at the time, and I had something to do with it. At that time Mr. Ilsley, as Minister of Finance, was responsible for old age pensions. Together with others I was pressing him for an end to this policy of making recoveries from the estates of deceased old age pensioners. As a result of those efforts and as a result of representations made to Mr. Ilsley by some of the provinces, the federal government finally took a stand. That stand was expressed in a letter written on March 23, 1944, and addressed to each of the provincial governments. On the same date the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), who was then parliamentary assistant to Mr. Ilsley, answered questions I had placed on the order paper, and in so doing told us what the government had done. I am looking at Hansard for March 23, 1944, pages 1742 and 1743. The questions are in my name; they relate to the filing of liens and the making of recoveries. The answer given by the then parliamentary assistant was rather lengthy. In it he quoted subsection 3 of section 9 of the Old Age Pensions Act, which said in part:
A pension authority shall be entitled to recover out of the estate of any deceased pensioner, as a debt due by the pensioner to such authority, the sum of the pension payments made to such pensioner-
Then the present Minister of Finance went on to say this, which is extremely significant:
There has been some legal doubt as to whether this clause was mandatory or permissive in its effect. For some time the dominion has followed the legal opinion that the section indicated an intention of the part of parliament that recoveries should be made and that as a matter of sound administration, it should be regarded as a statutory direction to the pension authorities to make recoveries in the ordinary course.
Now listen to this:
More recently we have been advised that while the drafting may leave some legal doubt, nevertheless the subsection is, strictly speaking, permissive. The provincial pension authorities have, as indicated in the answer to question 1. followed different policies, some have refused to follow the administrative requirement of making claims against the estates of deceased pensioners, others have suggested that it might be desirable either to discontinue making claims in all cases or to limit claims to the larger estates. In view of this situation, the provincial pension authorities are being advised that whether or not recovery should be made from estates where the net value does not exceed two thousand dollars will be left entirely to their discretion.

As I say, that was the answer given in this house to my questions as recorded in Hansard for March 23, 1944.
I now have in my hand sessional paper No. 89K, dated June 13, 1944, which was brought down in response to a motion of mine dealing with this matter. It includes a copy of a letter from Dr. Clark, the deputy minister of finance, to every province. I am sorry to tire the house with a good deal of the language I have just quoted, but it is important to get this matter straightened out. This letter says in part:
There has always been some legal doubt whether subsection 3 of section 9 of the act was mandatory or permissive in its effect. This department has, for some time, been following the legal opinion that the subsection indicates an intention on the part of parliament that recoveries should be made and that for administration purposes it should be regarded as statutory direction to the pension authorities to make recoveries in the ordinary course. Recently we have been advised that while the drafting may leave some legal doubt, nevertheless the subsection is, strictly speaking, permissive although the principle of sound administration may involve an obligation to make recoveries in the cases covered by the subsection.
Then, the last paragraph goes on to repeat much of what I have just quoted from the answer given in Hansard, which indicates that the federal government reached the conclusion that since the wording of that section was permissive rather than mandatory it was therefore saying to the provinces, "so far as we are concerned from now on you do not have to make any recoveries from estates where the value is less than $2,000." If the wording of that section of the federal act was found to be not mandatory but permissive, and on the basis of that situation it was possible for the federal government to say to the provinces, "you can ignore that part of the agreement, on estates of less than $2,000," I say that the federal government could say the same thing to the provinces today with respect to all estates.
The wording of the act is quite clear. In its original form, as it was enacted back in 1926 or 1927, it said:
A pension authority shall be entitled to recover out of the estate of any deceased pensioner . . .
and so on. It was thought for a time that that provision was mandatory, but it was finally ruled that it was permissive. The act was rewritten in 1947, and the phraseology was changed slightly. It was made to read along these lines.
An agreement made pursuant to section three of this act shall include an undertaking by the province that the pension authority will be authorized to recover out of the estate of any deceased pensioner . . .
It is mandatory that there shall be this provision in the agreement, but the provision 55704-35J
The Address-Mr. Knowles in the agreement is a permissive one, namely that the pension authority will be authorized to recover-authorized, but not compelled. I shall go along with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) this far, in that I think Mr. Schultz has put too strict an interpretation on the section in the act and the section in the agreement. I suppose what he is relying on is that letter received in 1944 telling them what they could do with estates of less than $2,000. He feels that until he gets a ruling from the federal government, he must abide by that ruling. Nevertheless, I feel that Mr. Schultz is not under any obligation to continue making these recoveries and I believe the minister agrees with me.
The whole section in that act was permissive, and the agreement under it was permissive. The legal opinion, as set out in Dr. Clark's letter of March 23, 1944, confirms the fact that it was permissive. I know from contacts I have had with members in different legislatures that in some other provinces the opposite view to the one taken by Mr. Schultz is being taken. In the meantime a great many old age pensioners in Manitoba are greatly worried. I think there should be the feast possible delay in clearing up this position. I am glad to know the minister is having this correspondence with the provinces. He might have told me that when he answered my question on March 12. Just telling me I had made a fine speech on the subject on the previous Monday was not a great deal of help, true though his comment may have been.

The Address-Mr. Knowles Manitoba, and I hope the minister will make such a statement to this house, to the country, to the provincial governments, and to Mr. Schultz in particular, at the earliest possible opportunity.
I should now like to speak on another matter. There has been a sharp [DOT] debate between the Liberal party and the C.C.F. during the last couple of weeks with respect to NATO. I do not wish to extend the debate on that question at this stage of our proceedings, but I believe it should foe pointed out that there is a great deal of unhappiness and uneasiness in the country over the secrecy that enshrouds the commitments made by NATO at Lisbon as well as at earlier meetings of that body. A good deal of the difference of opinion that has arisen in the course of this debate seems to stem from the fact that we do not yet know what the commitments were that this house allegedly supported a year ago, nor do we yet know the commitments that we will foe called upon to support at this session.
The minister has suggested to us that we supported such and such last year, and he frankly states that we have not yet been told what it was that we supported, particularly in terms of manpower. We now come to the situation this year, and when we question the advisability of the figure of $300 billion that is NATO's proposed military expenditure, he asks us where we got that figure. He knows that we got it from responsible newspapers which are being permitted to suggest that figure as the NATO goal. He questions it, yet he will not tell us what the precise goal is. I call upon the minister of external affairs to break through this secrecy. He owes it to this house and he owes it to the Canadian people to take us into his confidence and tell us what it is that is being planned so far as NATO is concerned. We feel that we have this coming to us in order that we might know precisely what is envisioned before we vote our share of any financial commitments, and also in order that we might be able to discuss the merits of one division or another as between money spent on military preparedness and money spent on economic aid to other countries.
I plead most strongly with the minister that he break through this secrecy and give us precise information about NATO just as soon as he possibly can. He must be aware of the fact that we are not the only ones asking for that information. He must be aware of the fact that members of all parties in this house are hoping he will give full details. He must be aware of the fact that

newspapers and magazines, even some periodicals that are critical of the stand we have taken, agree with us that we should have full information before we are asked to make commitments, and also in order that we may assess the division as between military preparedness and economic aid.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs knows quite well that we in this group support the principles of NATO; the house knows it; the country knows it. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, even the Winnipeg Free Press knows it. I mention the Winnipeg Free Press in particular because of a gross distortion in which that newspaper indulged on its editorial page on March 15. I do not have the page before me at the moment, but I have read it and I know what is there. We in Winnipeg are never surprised at any ideas that the Winnipeg Free Press may express in its editorial columns; but it is a matter of real amazement to me that on its editorial page the Winnipeg Free Press could run down those three centre columns material which it entitles "The Record", allegedly setting out clearly the statements that have been made by the various parties that have been discussing this matter, and yet so distort its presentation of that material. When you read something under the heading "The Record", you presume that if tells the whole story. And yet as one examines those three columns of material which are supposed to contain the record he finds, for example, that the statement issued by the C.C.F. national council has been decimated. The reference to our continuing support of NATO is deleted, our references to the need of economic aid, of what we are prepared to do in that field, are all wiped out. True, the Free Press protects itself by putting in a series of little dots here and there wherever omissions are made, but the end result is to completely distort the statement issued by the C.C.F. national council. As a matter of fact, the Free Press did the same thing with the remarks made in this house by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). They quote just part of what he said. They show by a few dots that they have left out something else that he said, but, as a matter of fact, to do so is to distort the impression that was given by the leader of the opposition to this house. It did the same with the remarks made by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the remarks made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Again, great sections are omitted and little dots are put in to indicate that to the reader of these three columns. That, I say, is a distortion of what is called "The Record", and I say to Mr. Grant Dexter, I am amazed that he has resorted to distortion

of that kind. I hope that at the earliest opportunity he will correct that, at least so far as this party is concerned, by reprinting on his editorial page in full the statement issued by the C.C.F. national council.
As I have already indicated, and as the Secretary of State for External Affairs knows, we support the principles of NATO. We accept the responsibility that it is laid upon us as a North Atlantic nation, within the framework of the United Nations, to build up defensive strength and at the same time to make arrangements for economic aid to the other members of the North Atlantic community, as well as to other countries throughout the world, with a view to achieving and establishing permanent peace. But surely it is our responsibility as members of this parliament, the parliament of one of the member countries of NATO, to consider very carefully the extent to which huge commitments for armaments and defence preparations might have a bearing on the economy of our country and of the other countries concerned. Surely it is up to us to discuss the extent to which we should spend money on armaments, as compared to the extent to which we should spend money on economic aid. Where we differ with the government, where we differ with the present NATO proposals, is in that division. We believe that too much is being spent on military preparations, and not enough on-economic aid to needy countries.
Now that the smoke of the smears and the slanders has been cleared away, we are asking that this house be given an opportunity to discuss this issue on its merits. I earnestly hope that in the debate on external affairs, which it is anticipated will commence as soon as this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne is over, the minister, in his very first statement, will take the house fully into his confidence and give us the facts so that we can deal with this important question in its proper light.
I want to say that although the minister's offer to hon. members who wish to have the figures at their disposal, to see those figures in confidence, was a thoughtful gesture on his part, I do not think it is the proper approach to this matter. I do not agree with the suggestion made in some newspapers that we should have a secret session. Rather, I think that any information that we are entitled to, on the basis of which we as members of this parliament should make our decisions, should be information available to the country as a whole, and I hope that something along that line will characterize the debate on this aspect of external affairs when we reach it after the end of this debate.
18, 1952
The Address-Mr. Knowles
Surely it is clear to all of us, Mr. Speaker, that the nations which belong to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization have had laid upon their shoulders one of the greatest responsibilities that has ever confronted any group of nations in the history of mankind. We have been called upon by events over which we have no control to go in for huge defence preparations. We have asserted that in building up these defence preparations it is our aim that they shall be purely and only defensive. We know, however, that never in the history of mankind has it been possible to build up huge armaments and prevent the outbreak of war. To avoid- such an outbreak is our task, and that is. the job that is laid at the door -of this nation and of all the nations that comprise the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. We must find a -balance between the amount of military preparation that will be defensive, and effectively defensive, without going so far as to cripple the economies of our nations and invite attack, and without establishing a military set-up that will provide the kind of provocation that leads to the war we seek to avoid.
Let us not forget that that is the aim of NATO: defensive preparation, but with it the idea set out in article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty, which calls- for the full use of that other weapon against aggression, which calls for that other means of building peace, namely, economic aid.
I hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the other ministers of the cabinet paid some attention to what their Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said in his speech over the week end. We were all interested in the simile that he drew upon when he said that NATO was a matter of insurance against war and that we should be prepared to pay the premium for such insurance. The Secretary of State for External Affairs kn-ows as well as we do-he has said it time and time again-that you do not fight communism only with bullets. You have got to fight it also with ideas; you have got to uproot the conditions that lead to communism; you have got to spread economic well-being throughout the world. That is one of the premiums that we have got to pay. How much willingness has this government shown to pay that premium? What support is the Secretary of State for External Affairs getting on that aspect of the matter, from his colleagues, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott)? So far as the proposals that he brings forward are concerned, it would look as though he is not getting any support at all on that score. It appears to us that his colleagues are not prepared to pay that part of

The Address-Mr. Courtemanche the premium for the insurance that we seek. But unless we do pay that premium the peace of the world is in jeopardy.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is a subject of importance second to none to all of us in Canada and to the whole world. I believe that the discussion which has arisen out of the statement made by the C.C.F. national council and the speeches made thus far by my leader, the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar, will in the end serve well the cause of peace, for what we are doing is asking that there be a critical examination of the whole situation, and in particular a critical approach to the whole question as to how we should divide our resources between military preparations and economic aid. We believe NATO's present spending is out of balance. At any rate, let us go into this question fully here in this parliament. Let us be met not with cocksureness on the government side that everything is right, particularly when we are not being told the full details of NATO's goals. Rather, let us have an honest consideration of the points we are making.
As I said before-and with this I close- we support the principles of NATO. We believe that it is the function of the North Atlantic treaty nations within the framework of the United Nations, within the framework of a world community, to do everything possible to prevent an outbreak of military hostilities, but we also believe it is their duty to go further and to build those social and economic conditions which will make possible the establishment of permanent peace.
